name: Battle of Dien Bien Phu
info: Viet Minh forces under Võ Nguyên Giáp besieged and overran a French Union garrison in the valley of Điện Biên Phủ in northwest Tonkin in 1954, in the First Indochina War, and French withdrawal from Indochina followed.

facts.place: The valley of Điện Biên Phủ, deep in the autonomous Tai Federation in northwest Tonkin, in present-day Vietnam, near the border with Laos
facts.sides: French Union forces under Colonel Christian de Castries, with 10,800 troops and reinforcements bringing the total to nearly 16,000; Viet Minh forces under General Võ Nguyên Giáp, with up to 50,000 regular troops in five divisions
facts.outcome: The garrison was overrun after a two-month siege and the survivors surrendered. French forces later withdrew from Indochina under the 1954 Geneva Accords, and Vietnam was temporarily divided at the 17th parallel.

t: The French built an isolated camp supplied by air in a valley whose surrounding high ground the Viet Minh controlled, and the Viet Minh brought in artillery and anti-aircraft guns that the French had not expected.

Casualty figures differ widely: the Vietnamese government reported 4,020 dead, 9,118 wounded and 792 missing, the French estimated 8,000 dead and 15,000 wounded, and Mark Moyar lists 22,900 out of 50,000.
Of 10,863 prisoners, including Vietnamese fighting for the French, only 3,290 were repatriated four months later; the death rate of French troops in captivity is estimated at about 60%.
dyk: Giáp's plan for a quick assault, due to open on 25 January 1954, was cancelled on 26 January after Viet Minh intelligence indicated that the French knew of it, and he later called the change of plan the hardest decision of his military career.
ev: Premier René Mayer names Henri Navarre to command French Union forces in Indochina
Operation Castor begins, and the French drop or fly 9,000 troops into Điện Biên Phủ over three days
The garrison of Lai Chau sets out for Điện Biên Phủ, and only 185 of its 2,100 men arrive by 22 December
The Viet Minh assault begins with an attack on the northeastern outpost of Béatrice
The Algerian battalion on Gabrielle falls back, abandoning the northern outpost to the Viet Minh
Massed Viet Minh assaults open on Dominique and Eliane in the central camp
The Viet Minh overrun Huguette 1 and take control of more than 90 percent of the airfield
Giáp orders an all-out attack and the remaining French positions are overrun

sections.background:
By 1953 the First Indochina War had passed through a succession of French commanders, among them Leclerc, de Lattre de Tassigny and Salan, none of whom had suppressed the insurrection of the Viet Minh, who were fighting for independence. In their 1952–1953 campaign the Viet Minh overran much of Laos, advancing as far as Luang Prabang and the Plain of Jars, and fell back only after outrunning their supply lines. In May 1953 Premier René Mayer named Henri Navarre to command French Union forces, with a single order: to create military conditions that would lead to an "honorable political solution".

Navarre looked for a way to meet the threat to Laos. Colonel Louis Berteil formulated the hérisson ('hedgehog') concept, a fortified airhead set up by airlift beside key Viet Minh supply lines to Laos, which would cut off the Viet Minh fighting there and force them to withdraw. It rested on the Battle of Nà Sản in late November and early December 1952, where the French had beaten back Giáp's forces repeatedly, inflicting very heavy losses. The French hoped to lure Giáp into a massed assault that their artillery, armour and air support could then decimate.

In June 1953 Major General René Cogny proposed Điện Biên Phủ, which had an old airstrip built by the Japanese, as a "mooring point". Cogny imagined a lightly defended base for raids, while Navarre believed he meant a heavily fortified one able to withstand a siege. Every major subordinate officer protested, and Cogny warned of "a new Nà Sản under worse conditions". Navarre rejected the criticism, called the hedgehog "a mediocre solution" and set the operation for 20 November 1953.
sections.forces:
Operation Castor began at 10:35 on 20 November 1953, when the French dropped or flew 9,000 troops into the valley over three days, together with a bulldozer to prepare the airstrip. From December, under Colonel Christian de Castries, they turned the camp into a fortress with seven satellite positions. The fortified headquarters stood in the centre, with Huguette to the west, Claudine to the south and Dominique to the northeast. The other positions were Anne-Marie to the northwest, Beatrice to the northeast, Gabrielle to the north and Isabelle, 6 km to the south, covering the reserve airstrip.

The garrison numbered 10,800 troops and, with further reinforcements, nearly 16,000. It had ten US M24 Chaffee light tanks, flown in in parts, artillery and aircraft, and included regular French troops, paratroopers, Foreign Legionnaires, Algerian and Moroccan tirailleurs and locally recruited Indochinese infantry. The Viet Minh moved up to 50,000 regular troops into the surrounding hills, five divisions including the 351st Heavy Division, an artillery formation. Their artillery and anti-aircraft guns outnumbered the French by about four to one. Giáp compared the valley to a "rice bowl", with his troops on the rim and the French at the bottom.

The Viet Minh had spent months stockpiling ammunition and siting guns in camouflaged casemates, and spies posing as camp labourers gave them the French artillery positions. The French garrison first came under direct artillery fire on 31 January 1954. Giáp had planned a fast assault on the Chinese "Fast Strike, Fast Victory" model, but cancelled it on 26 January and adopted "Steady Fight, Steady Advance", a siege approach.
sections.course:
The Viet Minh assault began on 13 March 1954 with a bombardment of Béatrice, held by the 3rd Battalion, 13th Foreign Legion Demi-Brigade. A shell killed the battalion commander, Major Paul Pégot, and most of his staff, and Lieutenant Colonel Jules Gaucher, commander of the central subsector, was killed soon after. The 312th Division then attacked, and Béatrice was not entirely taken until after 01:00 on 14 March. The French artillery commander, Colonel Charles Piroth, distraught at being unable to silence the camouflaged Viet Minh batteries, killed himself with a grenade two days later. The airstrip was put out of commission on 14 March, and supplies now had to come by parachute.

The Viet Minh attacked Gabrielle on the night of 14 March, and its Algerian battalion fell back the next morning. On 17 March most of the Tai troops on Anne-Marie left or defected. A lull followed until 30 March, in which the French suffered a crisis of command, and Isabelle was effectively cut off. On 30 March the Viet Minh captured Dominique 1 and 2 and Eliane 1, and fighting for Eliane and Dominique continued for days, with French counterattacks retaking and losing positions.

On 5 April Giáp changed to entrenchment and sapping. The French retook Eliane 1 on 10 and 11 April, but the Viet Minh overran Huguette 1 on 22 April and took more than 90 percent of the airfield. On 1 May they overran Eliane 1, Dominique 3 and Huguette 5. On 6 May they used Katyusha rockets and detonated a mine under Eliane 2. On 7 May Giáp ordered an all-out attack with over 25,000 men, and the last position, Lily, surrendered that night.
sections.aftermath:
On 8 May the Viet Minh counted 11,721 prisoners, of whom 4,436 were wounded, about one third of all those they had captured in the war. Able-bodied prisoners were force-marched more than 600 km to camps to the north and east, and hundreds died of disease on the way. The Red Cross extracted 858 of the wounded. Only around 200 French soldiers escaped, towards Luang Prabang. Of 10,863 prisoners, including Vietnamese fighting for the French, 3,290 were repatriated four months later, though the figure may include 3,013 prisoners of Vietnamese origin whose fate is unknown.

French casualties recorded until 5 May were 1,142 killed in action, 429 who died of wounds, 1,606 missing, 4,436 wounded and 1,161 deserters, not counting many more killed and wounded on 5, 6 and 7 May. Another source gives about 2,293 killed and 5,134 wounded. The Vietnamese government reported 4,020 dead, 9,118 wounded and 792 missing; the French estimated 8,000 dead and 15,000 wounded. Mark Moyar lists 22,900 out of 50,000.

The Geneva Conference opened on 8 May, the day after the surrender. The July agreement partitioned Vietnam into a communist North and the State of Vietnam, which opposed it. The elections meant to reunite the zones in 1956 were never held, and the last French forces left in 1956. In France the news caused shock, and Prime Minister Joseph Laniel resigned in June, replaced by Pierre Mendès France. In mid June the French ordered isolated positions abandoned, and Groupement Mobile 100 was ambushed at Mang Yang Pass.
sections.sources:
The surviving accounts are mostly by participants and later historians. Henri Navarre wrote of how Viet Minh commanders, under the influence of Chinese advisers, had dug in their artillery by single pieces and fired point-blank, which "was to make shambles of all the estimates" of French artillerymen. Phillip Davidson, a military scholar, described the state of French command that Navarre found on arrival. Bernard Fall, Martin Windrow and Jules Roy are cited on the events inside the camp. A commission under General Georges Catroux reported on the conduct of operations under Navarre.

Several points are disputed. Fall, using Colonel Pierre Langlais's memoirs, records that on 24 March Langlais and fellow paratroop commanders confronted de Castries in his bunker and took effective command. Davidson thought Langlais did take over effective command, while Roy does not mention the event and Windrow argues it is unlikely to have happened. Historians also disagree about the nickname "Angel of Điện Biên Phủ" for the flight nurse Geneviève de Galard: Windrow holds that the garrison used only her name, and Michael Kenney and Fall that press agencies added the nickname.

The casualty figures rest on different counts, and French and Vietnamese totals differ widely. Max Hastings stated that in 2018 Hanoi had still not credibly enumerated its losses. The French estimates of Viet Minh losses at Béatrice were 600 dead and 1,200 wounded, and the Viet Minh stated 193 killed and 137 wounded. The role of CIA controlled airlines was little known until Robbins published it after the Vietnam War and was not officially acknowledged until the 21st century.
sections.legacy:
Điện Biên Phủ was the decisive battle of the First Indochina War, and the loss of the garrison meant that roughly one tenth of French Union manpower in Indochina had been lost. The defeat did not significantly alter the strategic situation, but brought a profound psychological shock to France. The Catroux commission concluded that the fall was, in strictly military terms, a very serious failure that did not upset the balance of forces, and took on the aspect of definitive defeat through its effect on a French public tired of an unpopular war.

Outside Indochina the political significance was far-reaching. The Algerian National Liberation Front viewed it as an epoch-changing moment, and Ferhat Abbas, post-colonial Algeria's first president, called it "the 'Valmy' of the colonised peoples". Colonel William F. Long wrote twelve years later that Dien Bien Phu had become shorthand for a defeat of the West by the East. The United States, which was underwriting 80% of French expenditure in Indochina, had avoided overt intervention, though it covertly supplied pilots and aircraft.

In 1968 the North Vietnamese Army under Giáp besieged the US base at Khe Sanh, but there were differences: the Marines held the high ground, the supply base was 45 km away and Khe Sanh received 18,000 tons of air resupply in 77 days against 4,000 tons in 167 days at Điện Biên Phủ. Today the site is a popular tourist attraction with a modern museum, preserved French positions and memorials. The battle is the subject of Pierre Schoendoerffer's 1992 film Dien Bien Phu.

summary: From 13 March to 7 May 1954 the Viet Minh under Giáp besieged and overran the French camp at Điện Biên Phủ. The defeat shocked France, and the Geneva Accords then partitioned Vietnam temporarily at the 17th parallel.
notes: The article contradicts itself on weight: it calls the battle decisive and also says it did not significantly alter the strategic situation; both are given, with the Catroux commission's wording.

Casualty figures conflict (French killed 1,142 plus 429 recorded to 5 May, or about 2,293 killed and 5,134 wounded; Viet Minh 4,020 / 9,118 / 792, French 8,000 / 15,000, Moyar 22,900); the casualty paragraph of the article is garbled ('These figures were not include many more'). Prisoner counts: 11,721 captured but 10,863 in the repatriation figure.

The article says both that Eliane 1 was lost on 30 March (Viet Minh captured it) and, on 10 April, that it had been lost eleven days earlier; I wrote 30 March for Eliane 1 as the article's account of the 316th Division capturing it. Its text says Dominique 1 and 2 fell on 30 March too.

The de Castries 'paratrooper putsch' of 24 March is disputed (Fall, Davidson, Roy, Windrow); the Viet Minh morale and desertion details and the Béatrice losses are only French estimates against Viet Minh statements.
The article gives no section on sources as such; the sources section is built from the historians and documents it names, and is thin.

The article says the garrison was 10,800 'together with yet more reinforcements, totalling nearly 16,000' and the Viet Minh outnumbered the French four to one in troops but 'up to 50,000'; 16,000 against 50,000 is not four to one, so the ratio is given only for artillery.

Left out: the US involvement detail (nuclear weapons talk, CAT pilots' sorties), women at the camp, brothels, Berlioz and French mourning, the Mang Yang Pass and Chu Dreh Pass detail, the film Lost Command and the Billy Joel song.
